claim: HSPA2 is a member of the 70 kDa heat shock protein (HSP70) family.
source: Here, we demonstrate that the molecular chaperone heat shock protein A2 (HSPA2), a member of the 70 kDa heat shock protein (HSP70) family, is asymmetrically expressed in the late 2-cell stage of mouse embryos.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and introduction as an established characteristic of HSPA2.

claim: HSPA2 is asymmetrically expressed in the late 2-cell stage of mouse embryos.
source: Here, we demonstrate that the molecular chaperone heat shock protein A2 (HSPA2), a member of the 70 kDa heat shock protein (HSP70) family, is asymmetrically expressed in the late 2-cell stage of mouse embryos.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1H-J.

claim: The knockdown of Hspa2 in one of the 2-cell blastomeres prevented its progeny predominantly towards the inner cell mass (ICM) fate.
source: The knockdown of Hspa2 in one of the 2-cell blastomeres prevented its progeny predominantly towards the inner cell mass (ICM) fate.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in Figure 3.

claim: The overexpression of Hspa2 in one of the 2-cell blastomeres did not induce the blastomere to differentiate towards the ICM fate.
source: In contrast, the overexpression of Hspa2 in one of the 2-cell blastomeres did not induce the blastomere to differentiate towards the ICM fate.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in Figure 4.

claim: HSPA2 interacts with CARM1.
source: Furthermore, we demonstrated that HSPA2 interacted with CARM1 and its levels correlated with ICM-associated genes.
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 5F and G.

claim: HSPA2 levels correlate with ICM-associated genes.
source: Furthermore, we demonstrated that HSPA2 interacted with CARM1 and its levels correlated with ICM-associated genes.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing correlation between Hspa2 and Nanog expression (Figure 1C).

claim: The first cell-fate decision occurs at the morula stage following embryonic compaction.
source: Specifically, the first cell-fate decision occurs at the morula stage following embryonic compaction and results in the division of embryonic cells into two distinct lineages: the trophectoderm (TE) and the inner cell mass (ICM).
evidence: This is established knowledge about mammalian embryonic development.

claim: The first cell-fate decision results in the division of embryonic cells into two distinct lineages: the trophectoderm (TE) and the inner cell mass (ICM).
source: Specifically, the first cell-fate decision occurs at the morula stage following embryonic compaction and results in the division of embryonic cells into two distinct lineages: the trophectoderm (TE) and the inner cell mass (ICM).
evidence: This is established knowledge about mammalian embryonic development, supported by citations.

claim: The TE is a single layer surrounding the fluid-filled cavity known as the blastocoel that provides extraembryonic structures such as the placenta.
source: The TE is a single layer surrounding the fluid-filled cavity known as the blastocoel that provides extraembryonic structures such as the placenta, whereas the ICM, which is attached to the inside of the TE, contains pluripotent cells that give rise to the fetus and extraembryonic tissues (Cockburn and Rossant, 2010; Liu et al., 2021; Rossant and Tam, 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The ICM is attached to the inside of the TE and contains pluripotent cells that give rise to the fetus and extraembryonic tissues.
source: The TE is a single layer surrounding the fluid-filled cavity known as the blastocoel that provides extraembryonic structures such as the placenta, whereas the ICM, which is attached to the inside of the TE, contains pluripotent cells that give rise to the fetus and extraembryonic tissues (Cockburn and Rossant, 2010; Liu et al., 2021; Rossant and Tam, 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: CARM1 exhibits asymmetric nuclear abundance at the 4-cell stage.
source: The asymmetry of the blastocyst may be traced back to the asymmetric nuclear abundance of coactivator-associated arginine methyltransferase 1 (CARM1) at the 4-cell stage (Goolam et al., 2016; Shi et al., 2015; Torres-Padilla et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies, supported by citations.

claim: The heterogeneous activity of CARM1 leads to the differential methylation of H3R26me.
source: The heterogeneous activity of CARM1 leads to the differential methylation of H3 methylation of arginine 26 (H3R26me).
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies.

claim: More extensive methylation of H3R26me can result in a higher increase in the expression levels of ICM-specific genes (e.g. Pou5f1, Nanog and Sox2) and global chromatin accessibility, which direct their progeny into the ICM fate.
source: More extensive methylation of H3R26me can result in a higher increase in the expression levels of ICM-specific genes (e.g. Pou5f1, Nanog and Sox2) and global chromatin accessibility, which direct their progeny into the ICM fate (Sotomayor-Lugo et al., 2024).
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies, supported by citation.

claim: Gm45001 (LincGET) is asymmetrically expressed in the nuclei of blastomeres in 2- and 4-cell embryos.
source: For example, a long non-coding RNA, Gm45001 (LincGET), is known to be asymmetrically expressed in the nuclei of blastomeres in 2- and 4-cell embryos.
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies.

claim: Gm45001 and CARM1 form a complex that promotes H3R26me and activates the expression of ICM genes.
source: Specifically, Gm45001 and CARM1 are known to form a complex that promotes H3R26me and activates the expression of ICM genes (Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies, supported by citation.

claim: HMGA1 exhibits heterogeneity as early as the 2-cell stage and is involved in cell fate differentiation.
source: In addition, HMGA1, a member of the high mobility group (HMG) protein family, is also known to exhibit heterogeneity as early as the 2-cell stage and involves in cell fate differentiation (Wang et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies, supported by citation.

claim: HSPA2 is originally identified in male germ cells and described as a testis-specific protein that is essential for spermatogenesis.
source: It is originally identified in male germ cells and described as a testis-specific protein that is essential for spermatogenesis (Gómez-Torres et al., 2023; Scieglinska and Krawczyk, 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies, supported by citations.

claim: The Hspa2 gene is located on chromosome 14 (14q24.1).
source: The Hspa2 gene is located on chromosome 14 (14q24.1) (Zhang et al., 2013), and the aberrant expression of HSPA2 in testes was shown to induce primary spermatocytes to arrest in meiosis I and undergo apoptosis, thus leading to male infertility (Bonnycastle et al., 1994; Dix et al., 1996).
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies, supported by citation.

claim: The aberrant expression of HSPA2 in testes induces primary spermatocytes to arrest in meiosis I and undergo apoptosis, leading to male infertility.
source: The Hspa2 gene is located on chromosome 14 (14q24.1) (Zhang et al., 2013), and the aberrant expression of HSPA2 in testes was shown to induce primary spermatocytes to arrest in meiosis I and undergo apoptosis, thus leading to male infertility (Bonnycastle et al., 1994; Dix et al., 1996).
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies, supported by citations.

claim: HSPA2 is expressed in somatic tissues and during mouse embryogenesis.
source: HSPA2 is expressed in somatic tissues and during mouse embryogenesis (Murashov and Wolgemuth, 1996; Rupik et al., 2006), and high levels of HSPA2 expression play a critical role in the genesis and progression of carcinoma (Garg et al., 2010a; Garg et al., 2010b).
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies, supported by citations.

claim: High levels of HSPA2 expression play a critical role in the genesis and progression of carcinoma.
source: HSPA2 is expressed in somatic tissues and during mouse embryogenesis (Murashov and Wolgemuth, 1996; Rupik et al., 2006), and high levels of HSPA2 expression play a critical role in the genesis and progression of carcinoma (Garg et al., 2010a; Garg et al., 2010b).
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies, supported by citations.

claim: Hspa2 mRNA is stored maternally at the MII oocyte and decreases at the two-cell stage.
source: qRT-PCR analysis showed that Hspa2 mRNA was stored maternally at the MII oocyte and decreased at the two-cell stage but remarkably increased from the 2-cell to the 4-cell stage, coinciding with zygotic genome activation (ZGA).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Hspa2 mRNA remarkably increases from the 2-cell to the 4-cell stage, coinciding with zygotic genome activation (ZGA).
source: qRT-PCR analysis showed that Hspa2 mRNA was stored maternally at the MII oocyte and decreased at the two-cell stage but remarkably increased from the 2-cell to the 4-cell stage, coinciding with zygotic genome activation (ZGA).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Hspa2 expression shows a slight change as embryos develop to the 8-cell and morula stages.
source: There was a slight change in expression as embryos developed to the 8-cell and morula stages, and developed into blastocysts that had higher expression levels than the 2-cell stage (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Blastocysts have higher Hspa2 expression levels than the 2-cell stage.
source: There was a slight change in expression as embryos developed to the 8-cell and morula stages, and developed into blastocysts that had higher expression levels than the 2-cell stage (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: HSPA2 is symmetrically distributed between the two blastomeres at the early 2-cell stage.
source: For the early 2-cell stage, however, HSPA2 was symmetrically distributed between the two blastomeres (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–E.

claim: The heterogeneity of HSPA2 occurred as early as the late 2-cell stage.
source: These results indicate that the heterogeneity occurred as early as the late 2-cell stage.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing symmetric distribution at early 2-cell and asymmetric distribution at late 2-cell stage.

claim: The blastocyst formation rate in the Hspa2-KD group (52.3 ± 2.5%) was significantly lower than that in the NC group (81.6 ± 2.0%).
source: Furthermore, the blastocyst formation rate in the Hspa2-KD group (52.3 ± 2.5%) was significantly lower than that in the NC group (81.6 ± 2.0%; Figure 2G and H), thus suggesting that HSPA2 plays an essential role in preimplantation embryonic development.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G and H.

claim: HSPA2 plays an essential role in preimplantation embryonic development.
source: Furthermore, the blastocyst formation rate in the Hspa2-KD group (52.3 ± 2.5%) was significantly lower than that in the NC group (81.6 ± 2.0%; Figure 2G and H), thus suggesting that HSPA2 plays an essential role in preimplantation embryonic development.
evidence: This is an inference based on the reduced blastocyst formation rate upon Hspa2 knockdown.

claim: The down-regulation of Hspa2 results in a remarkable down-regulation of specific ICM-marker genes (Pou5f1, Sox2, and Nanog) at the 4 cell and blastocyst stages.
source: In addition, we found that the down-regulation of Hspa2 resulted in a remarkable down-regulation of specific ICM-marker genes (Pou5f1, Sox2, and Nanog) at the 4 cell and blastocyst stages.
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR and western blot data shown in Figure 2I-L.

claim: The mRNA levels of the TE-marker gene Cdx2 did not significantly change between the Hspa2-KD and NC groups.
source: Meanwhile, the mRNA levels of a TE-marker gene, Cdx2, did not significantly change between the groups (Figure 2I and J).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2I and J.

claim: The expression levels of ICM-marker proteins (OCT4 and SOX2) were inhibited when HSPA2 was down-regulated at the 4-cell and blastocyst stages.
source: We then used automated western immunoblotting to detect the protein levels of ICM and TE markers in Hspa2-KD embryos, and found that the expression levels of ICM-marker proteins (OCT4 and SOX2) were inhibited when HSPA2 was down-regulated at the 4cell and blastocyst stages, while the TE-marker protein CDX2 was not significantly different between the groups (Figure 2K and L).
evidence: This is supported by automated western blotting data shown in Figure 2K and L.

claim: The TE-marker protein CDX2 was not significantly different between the Hspa2-KD and NC groups at the 4-cell and blastocyst stages.
source: We then used automated western immunoblotting to detect the protein levels of ICM and TE markers in Hspa2-KD embryos, and found that the expression levels of ICM-marker proteins (OCT4 and SOX2) were inhibited when HSPA2 was down-regulated at the 4cell and blastocyst stages, while the TE-marker protein CDX2 was not significantly different between the groups (Figure 2K and L).
evidence: This is supported by automated western blotting data shown in Figure 2K and L.

claim: The knockdown of HSPA2 in mESCs resulted in a significant reduction for the ICM-marker proteins, and no change for CDX2.
source: Similarly, for mouse embryonic stem cells (mESCs), the knockdown of HSPA2 resulted in a significant reduction for the ICM-marker proteins, and no change for CDX2 (Figure 2M).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2M.

claim: The number of ICM and total cells in the blastocyst were significantly decreased in the Hspa2-KD group, but the number of TE cells did not change significantly.
source: It was showed that the number of ICM and total cells in the blastocyst were significantly decreased, but the number of TE cells did not change significantly (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: The GFP +Hspa2 KD group (33.8 %±4.3%) exhibited a significantly reduced ratio of progeny cells with an ICM fate compared with the GFP +NC group (48.2% ± 7.4%).
source: Compared with the GFP +NC group (48.2% ± 7.4%), the GFP +Hspa2 KD group (33.8 %±4.3%) exhibited a significantly reduced ratio of progeny cells with an ICM fate.
evidence: This is supported by lineage tracing data shown in Figure 3D and E.

claim: The number of ICM-marker OCT4 positive cells was significantly reduced in the GFP +Hspa2 KD group (27.1 ± 3.8%) than in the GFP +NC group (37.0% ± 2.5%).
source: Moreover, the number of ICM-marker OCT4 positive cells was found to be significantly reduced in the GFP +Hspa2 KD group (27.1 ± 3.8%) than in the GFP +NC group (37.0% ± 2.5%; Figure 3D and E).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3D and E.

claim: HSPA2 has a role in ICM lineage establishment and its deficiency leads to partial defects in the ICM cells.
source: Collectively, these results suggested that HSPA2 has a role in ICM lineage establishment and its deficiency leads to partial defects in the ICM cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing reduced ICM cells upon Hspa2 knockdown.

claim: The blastocyst formation rate was not affected significantly by overexpression of Hspa2.
source: However, we observed that the blastocyst formation rate was not affected significantly (Figure 4A and B), thus showing that the overexpression of Hspa2 did not exert adverse effects on embryonic development.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: The overexpression of Hspa2 did not exert adverse effects on embryonic development.
source: However, we observed that the blastocyst formation rate was not affected significantly (Figure 4A and B), thus showing that the overexpression of Hspa2 did not exert adverse effects on embryonic development.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that blastocyst formation rate was not affected.

claim: The mRNA levels of the ICM-marker genes (Pou5f1, Sox2, and Nanog) and the TE-marker gene Cdx2 at the 4 cell and blastocyst stage did not differ significantly between Hspa2 overexpression and control groups.
source: In addition, we verified that the mRNA levels of the ICM-marker genes (Pou5f1, Sox2, and Nanog) and the TE-marker gene Cdx2 at the 4 cell and blastocyst stage did not differ significantly (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4C and D.

claim: The number of ICM and TE cells were not altered significantly between Hspa2 overexpression and control groups.
source: We also examined the number of ICM and TE cells by immunostaining OCT4 and CDX2 in blastocysts from the overexpression and control groups and found they were not altered significantly (Figure 4E and F).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4E and F.

claim: The percentage of GFP cells that were present in the ICM at the blastocyst stage was similar between the Hspa2 overexpression and control groups (48.2±7.4 vs 47.3±4.4).
source: We found that the percentage of GFP cells that were present in the ICM at the blastocyst stage was similar between the two groups (48.2±7.4 vs 47.3±4.4), and the percentage of ICM cells also did not differ significantly (37.0±2.5 vs 36.2±1.9; Figure 4G and H).
evidence: This is supported by lineage tracing data shown in Figure 4G and H.

claim: The redundant level of HSPA2 was not sufficient to induce blastomere cells to bias an ICM fate.
source: These observations indicated that the redundant level of HSPA2 was not sufficient to induce blastomere cells to bias an ICM fate.
evidence: This is an inference based on the overexpression experiments showing no change in ICM fate.

claim: CARM1 is the first protein arginine methyltransferase which was proved to be associated with transcriptional activation by methylating and/or regulating histone H3 and non-histone proteins.
source: Coactivator-associated arginine methyltransferase 1 (CARM1), also known as PRMT4, is the first protein arginine methyltransferase which was proved to be associated with transcriptional activation by methylating and/or regulating histone H3 and non-histone proteins, such as coactivators and transcription factors (Stallcup et al., 2003; Troffer-Charlier et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies, supported by citations.

claim: CARM1 regulates early mouse development and plays a role in the determination of cell fate.
source: Recent studies have demonstrated that CARM1 regulates early mouse development and plays a role in the determination of cell fate (Hupalowska et al., 2018; Pawlak et al., 2000).
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies, supported by citations.

claim: CARM1 levels, along with its specific histone marks (H3R17me2a and H3R26me2a), vary among the 4-cell blastomeres.
source: CARM1 levels, along with its specific histone marks (H3R17me2a and H3R26me2a), were found to vary among the 4-cell blastomeres and that high levels of CARM1 led to increased levels of H3R26me.
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies.

claim: High levels of CARM1 led to increased levels of H3R26me.
source: CARM1 levels, along with its specific histone marks (H3R17me2a and H3R26me2a), were found to vary among the 4-cell blastomeres and that high levels of CARM1 led to increased levels of H3R26me.
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies.

claim: The varied distribution of CARM1 led to biased subsequent fate of the blastomeres towards the ICM.
source: This varied distribution led to biased subsequent fate of the blastomeres towards the ICM (Parfitt and Zernicka-Goetz, 2010; Torres-Padilla et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies, supported by citations.

claim: HSPA2 docks efficiently with CARM1 via several H-bonds and pi-interactions, with strong binding affinity.
source: Molecular docking revealed that HSPA2 docked efficiently with CARM1 via several H-bonds and pi-interactions, with strong binding affinity (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by molecular docking analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: HSPA2, CARM1, and ICM-specific proteins interact with each other according to STRING database prediction.
source: The Search Tool for the Retrieval of Interacting Genes (STRING) database was used to predict interactions between HSPA2 and CARM1. The results showed that HSPA2, CARM1, and ICM-specific proteins interacted with each other (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by STRING database analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1F.

claim: The Hspa2-KD led to reduced CARM1 mRNA as well as protein levels at the 4 cell and blastocyst stages.
source: In addition, we found that the Hspa2-KD led to reduced CARM1 mRNA as well as protein levels at the 4 cell and blastocyst stages (Figure 5B–E).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR and western blot data shown in Figure 5B–E.

claim: The knockdown of HSPA2 in mESCs caused a significant reduction in the levels of CARM1.
source: The knockdown of HSPA2 in mESCs also caused a significant reduction in the levels of CARM1 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1G.

claim: HSPA2 and CARM1 proteins interact effectively as shown by co-IP analysis.
source: Co-IP analysis showed that HSPA2 and CARM1 proteins interacted effectively (Figure 5F and G).
evidence: This is supported by co-IP data shown in Figure 5F and G.

claim: CARM1-mediated H3R26me2 levels were significantly reduced in the Hspa2 interference group at the 4-cell stage.
source: Immunofluorescence staining confirmed that CARM1-mediated H3R26me2 levels were significantly reduced in the interference group at the 4-cell stage (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: HSPA2 is involved in the segregation of embryonic cell lineage by forming a complex with CARM1 and through H3R26me2 modification.
source: Collectively, our data demonstrated that HSPA2 involved in the segregation of embryonic cell lineage by forming a complex with CARM1 and through H3R26me2 modification.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing HSPA2-CARM1 interaction and effects on H3R26me2.

claim: Molecular polarity and differential gene regulation by signaling pathways drive the first cell-fate decision in mammals.
source: Previous studies demonstrated that molecular polarity and differential gene regulation by signaling pathways drive the first cell-fate decision in mammals (Hirate and Sasaki, 2014; Johnson and Ziomek, 1981; Korotkevich et al., 2017; Nishioka et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies, supported by citations.

claim: The cellular heterogeneity is initiated early in the embryo according to the cellular heterogeneity hypothesis.
source: The tracing of embryonic lineages from the 2-cell stage onwards by live embryo labeling demonstrated that the cellular heterogeneity is initiated early in the embryo, and thus was proposed as cellular heterogeneity hypothesis (Piotrowska and Zernicka-Goetz, 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies, supported by citation.

claim: When 2-cell blastomeres are separated, in the majority of cases, only one of the two blastomeres develops into a mouse.
source: Although 2-cell blastomeres are generally considered to be totipotent, the previous reports showing that when 2-cell blastomeres are separated, in the majority of cases, only one of the two blastomeres develops into a mouse (Casser et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies, supported by citation.

claim: The heterogeneity of HSPA2 at the late 2-cell embryo may be initiated concomitant with the zygotic genome activation (ZGA).
source: This indicates that the heterogeneity of HSPA2 at the late 2-cell embryo may be initiated concomitant with the zygotic genome activation (ZGA) (Shi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is speculation based on the timing of HSPA2 heterogeneity appearance and ZGA, supported by citation.

claim: The asymmetry of HSPA2 may be triggered by unequally distributed unknown factors that already existed in the early 2-cell embryos or the heterogeneous spatial distribution of maternal genes in the zygote.
source: Alternatively, the asymmetry may be triggered by unequally distributed unknown factors that already existed in the early 2-cell embryos or the heterogeneous spatial distribution of maternal genes in the zygote.
evidence: This is speculation about possible mechanisms for HSPA2 asymmetry.

claim: Knockdown of HSPA2 results in lower cell number in ICM by interfering with the cell cycle.
source: Hspa2 knockdown via siRNA reduced cell proliferation and led to G1/S phase cell cycle arrest (Cao et al., 2019). Thus, we hypothesized that knockdown of HSPA2 results in lower cell number in ICM by interfering with the cell cycle.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on previous findings and current observations, supported by citation.

claim: The lower cell number in ICM may also be associated with failed cytokinesis and the generation of binucleated or polyploid cells.
source: Additionally, the lower cell number in ICM may also associated with failed cytokinesis and the generation of binucleated or polyploid cells.
evidence: This is speculation about possible mechanisms for reduced ICM cell number.

claim: Half of the ICM cells still formed with HSPA2 deficiency, possibly due to the incomplete knockdown achieved or the possibility that redundant pathways exist.
source: Interestingly, half of the ICM cells still formed with HSPA2 deficiency (Figure 3B), possibly due to the incomplete knockdown achieved or the possibility that redundant pathways exist.
evidence: This is speculation about why ICM cells still form despite HSPA2 knockdown.

claim: Once the intracellular concentration of Hspa2 reaches a threshold level, it was not able to control the target gene expression.
source: It may be because that once the intracellular concentration of Hspa2 reaches a threshold level, it was not able to control the target gene expression.
evidence: This is speculation about why overexpression of Hspa2 does not affect ICM fate.

claim: The DEGs at blastocyst stage with HSPA2 knocking down were enriched in Wnt signaling pathway and Hippo signaling pathway.
source: In fact, our RNA-seq results revealed that the DEGs at blastocyst stage with HSPA2 knocking down were also enriched in Wnt signaling pathway and Hippo signaling pathway (Figure 2E), which are also reported to be involved in cell proliferation, cell polarity, and cell fate determination during embryonic development (Nishioka et al., 2009; Morris et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2E and established knowledge from citations.

claim: Wnt signaling pathway and Hippo signaling pathway are involved in cell proliferation, cell polarity, and cell fate determination during embryonic development.
source: In fact, our RNA-seq results revealed that the DEGs at blastocyst stage with HSPA2 knocking down were also enriched in Wnt signaling pathway and Hippo signaling pathway (Figure 2E), which are also reported to be involved in cell proliferation, cell polarity, and cell fate determination during embryonic development (Nishioka et al., 2009; Morris et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies, supported by citations.

claim: Several alternative mechanisms are compatible with the asymmetric hypothesis, including polarized cell division and differential gene regulation by signaling.
source: This indicates that several alternative mechanisms are compatible with the asymmetric hypothesis, including polarized cell division and differential gene regulation by signaling.
evidence: This is an inference based on the RNA-seq results showing enrichment in multiple signaling pathways.

claim: The mRNA and protein levels of HSPA2 differ among the four blastomeres at the 4-cell stage.
source: The results showed that the mRNA and protein levels of HSPA2 differed among the four blastomeres (Figure 1E and F), and confirmed by fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) analysis (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by single-cell qRT-PCR, automated western blotting, and FISH data shown in Figure 1E-G.

claim: In total, 96 up-regulated genes and 410 down-regulated genes were identified in the Hspa2-KD group when compared to the NC group.
source: In total, 96 up-regulated genes and 410 down-regulated genes were identified in the Hspa2-KD group when compared to the NC group (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: The most significant GO enriched terms were closely related to cell fate commitment, stem cell population maintenance, stem cell differentiation and blastocyst development.
source: The most significant GO enriched terms were closely related to cell fate commitment, stem cell population maintenance, stem cell differentiation and blastocyst development (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by GO enrichment analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: According to KEGG analysis, the down-regulated genes were primarily associated with Hippo and Wnt signaling pathways.
source: According to KEGG analysis, the down-regulated genes were primarily associated with Hippo and Wnt signaling pathways (Figure 2F), which are known to play an important role in cell proliferation, differentiation, and fate decisions in embryonic development (de Jaime-Soguero et al., 2018; Nishioka et al., 2009; Świerczek Lasek et al., 2021; ten Berge et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by KEGG enrichment analysis shown in Figure 2F and established knowledge from citations.

claim: Hippo and Wnt signaling pathways play an important role in cell proliferation, differentiation, and fate decisions in embryonic development.
source: According to KEGG analysis, the down-regulated genes were primarily associated with Hippo and Wnt signaling pathways (Figure 2F), which are known to play an important role in cell proliferation, differentiation, and fate decisions in embryonic development (de Jaime-Soguero et al., 2018; Nishioka et al., 2009; Świerczek Lasek et al., 2021; ten Berge et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies, supported by citations.

claim: Knock-down Hspa2 in one blastomere at the 2-cell stage led to developmental defects.
source: Knock-down Hspa2 in one blastomere at the 2-cell stage also led to developmental defects (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: A total of 43 annotated DEPs were identified by proteomics, of which 15 proteins were significantly up-regulated and 28 proteins were down-regulated.
source: Volcano map screening identified a total of 43 annotated DEPs, of which 15 proteins were significantly up-regulated and 28 proteins were down-regulated (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by proteomics data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: DEPs were mainly involved in post-translational modification according to COG/KOG functional annotation statistics.
source: These DEPs were mainly involved in post-translational modification by using Clusters of Orthologous Groups (COG)/Karyotic Orthologous Groups (KOG) functional annotation statistics (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by COG/KOG analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Biological processes analysis showed that DEPs were associated with positive regulation of the Wnt signaling pathway and cellular development.
source: Biological processes analysis showed that DEPs were associated with positive regulation of the Wnt signaling pathway and cellular development (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by GO analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: In terms of the cellular component, the DEPs were related to the methylome and methyltransferase complex.
source: In terms of the cellular component, the DEPs were related to the methylome and methyltransferase complex (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by GO analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The DEPs were mainly associated with the post-translational modification of proteins and cell fate decision.
source: These results indicated that the DEPs were mainly associated with the post-translational modification of proteins and cell fate decision.
evidence: This is an inference based on the proteomics and GO analysis results.

claim: Hspa2 mRNA is heterogeneously distributed at the late 2-cell and 4-cell embryos after microinjection of siHspa2 in zygotes.
source: Interestingly, Hspa2 mRNA also heterogeneous distribution at the late 2-cell and 4-cell embryos after microinjection of si-Hspa2 in zygotes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F, G).
evidence: This is supported by single-cell qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F, G.
